blocks.content: Have you ever played a game with thousands of trees on the map?
Every tree looks the same texture, same color, same shape. Only their position is different.
Now imagine creating a brand new object for every single tree, storing all that data thousands of times over.
Your app would run out of memory.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245782493-912d1dd4.png
That reusable shared design is the Flyweight.
1. The Problem: Rendering Trees
Imagine you're building an open world game that needs to render trees on screen something like Minecraft or any city builder.
Every tree on screen needs rendering properties like: tree type, color, texture.
On top of that, each tree has its own position on the map (its x and y coordinates).
The straightforward approach is to create a full object for every tree, bundling all this data together. Here is what the naive code looks like:

codes.python:
class Tree:
    # Naive design: every tree stores a full copy of type, color and texture.
    def __init__(self, tree_type, color, texture, x, y):
        self.type = tree_type       # e.g. "Oak", "Pine"
        self.color = color          # e.g. "green"
        self.texture = texture      # e.g. "bark.png"
        self.x = x                  # position X
        self.y = y                  # position Y

    def render(self):
        print(f"Rendering {self.type} tree | color: {self.color} texture: {self.texture} at ({self.x},{self.y})")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Naive approach: every tree gets its own full copy of type/color/texture
    t1 = Tree("Oak", "green", "bark.png", 100, 200)
    t2 = Tree("Oak", "green", "bark.png", 300, 150)
    t3 = Tree("Pine", "darkgreen", "pine.png", 200, 300)

    t1.render()
    t2.render()
    t3.render()

blocks.content: Now imagine an open world map with 50,000 trees. Each tree carries its own copy of type, color, and texture. Yet most trees share the exact same properties. That is a massive amount of wasted memory.
Why This Is a Problem?
The naive design works fine for a small map. But as the world grows, serious problems appear.
1. High Memory Usage

Every tree object stores its own copy of type, color, and texture. In a typical game map, most trees share identical data. If each object takes roughly 100 bytes of rendering data, a 50,000-tree map wastes around 5MB on duplicated information alone.
The actual position only needs 8 bytes per tree. Everything else is pure redundancy.
2. Performance Bottleneck
Creating and managing 50,000 individual objects puts enormous pressure on memory. Each object sits on the heap. The garbage collector has to track, scan, and collect all of them.
On lower-end devices this causes visible lag, frame drops, and stuttering during gameplay especially when new areas of the map load in.
3. Poor Scalability
One small map is just the beginning. What about a larger world with forests, jungles, and plains? Or multiple maps loaded at once?
Memory usage multiplies with every new area. What worked in a small prototype becomes completely unworkable at real game scale.
4. No State Separation
The core issue is that intrinsic state and extrinsic state are tangled together in every object.

Extrinsic state (x and y position) unique to each tree

blocks.content: By lumping them into one object, every tree becomes unique even when only the position differs. There is no way to share what can be shared.
What We Really Need

["Share rendering data (type, color, texture) among all trees that look the same","Store only truly unique data (position) per tree instance","Avoid duplicating redundant data while still rendering every tree accurately","Use a central factory to manage and cache shared instances"]
items: Share rendering data (type, color, texture) among all trees that look the same
Store only truly unique data (position) per tree instance
Avoid duplicating redundant data while still rendering every tree accurately
Use a central factory to manage and cache shared instances

blocks.content: This is exactly what the Flyweight Pattern solves.
2. What is the Flyweight Pattern

The Flyweight Pattern is a structural design pattern that minimizes memory usage by sharing common state across a large number of similar objects instead of storing that state in each object individually.
Two characteristics define the Flyweight Pattern and set it apart from other structural patterns:
1. Intrinsic/Extrinsic State Separation

The pattern splits object state into two parts. Intrinsic state is shared and immutable stored inside the flyweight. Extrinsic state is unique per instance stored outside and passed in at runtime. This separation is what makes sharing possible.

Intrinsic  →  type, color, texture   (stored ONCE, shared by all trees)
Extrinsic  →  x, y position          (unique per tree, passed in at render time)

blocks.content: 2. Factory-Managed Caching
A dedicated factory controls the creation and reuse of flyweights. Clients never create flyweights directly.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245782608-a2f6f38f.png
They ask the factory, which checks its cache first if the tree type already exists, it returns the same object. No duplicates, ever.

Client asks: "Give me an Oak tree"
Factory checks cache → already exists → returns same Oak object 

Client asks again:   "Give me an Oak tree"
Factory checks cache → returns same Oak object again (not a new one)

blocks.content: What Each Part Does
TreeFlyweight Interface declares render(x, y) which takes the extrinsic state (position) as a parameter.
ConcreteTree implements the flyweight and stores intrinsic state: type, color, and texture. This object is created once and reused thousands of times.

TreeFactory holds a cache of all created tree types. When the client asks for an Oak, it checks the cache first. If Oak already exists, it returns it. If not, it creates it, stores it, and returns it.
Client holds only the extrinsic state (x, y positions). It never creates trees directly. It asks the factory and calls render(x, y) with the position.
The Key Insight

Without Flyweight:
50,000 trees = 50,000 full objects in memory 

With Flyweight:
50,000 trees = 3 shared objects + 50,000 lightweight positions

3. Implementing the Flyweight Pattern

Let's implement the Flyweight Pattern to optimize how we render trees in an open world game. Our goal is to share common rendering properties (type, color, texture) across trees and store only unique data (position) at the instance level.

The fix is to split each tree into two parts: the rendering data that can be shared (intrinsic state) and the position that is unique to each tree (extrinsic state). A factory manages the shared objects, and the client combines them with position data at render time.
Step 1: Define the Flyweight Interface

The flyweight interface declares a single method render(x, y) where x and y represent extrinsic state. The flyweight itself does not store position. The caller passes position in at render time. This is the key decision that makes sharing possible.

Every flyweight object implements this interface. The client calls render with any position, and the flyweight combines that position with its stored rendering data. One flyweight instance can serve thousands of trees.
Step 2: Implement the Concrete Flyweight
The concrete flyweight stores intrinsic state only: tree type, color, and texture. These fields are immutable. Once created, they never change.
Notice the constructor takes only three parameters position is completely gone from the object's state. The finalmodifiers mean these fields are set once and never change.
This immutability is what makes sharing safe. No matter how many clients reference the same flyweight, none of them can corrupt it.
Step 3: Create the Flyweight Factory

The factory maintains a map of already-created flyweights, keyed by a string combining all intrinsic fields. When a client requests a tree type, the factory checks the cache first. If it exists, it returns the same instance. If not, it creates one, stores it, and returns it.

The factory guarantees that if two trees share the same type, color, and texture, they point to the exact same object in memory. getTreeTypeCount() is useful for verifying how much sharing actually occurred.
Step 4: Create the Client

The client has two parts. PlacedTree is a lightweight wrapper pairing a shared flyweight with a specific position. GameMapClient is the main orchestrator it uses the factory to get flyweights, wraps them with position data, and renders the entire map.

Each PlacedTree is extremely lightweight just a reference to a shared flyweight and two integers. The heavy rendering data lives in the flyweight, and thousands of PlacedTree instances point to the same one. This is where the memory savings come from.

What We Achieved
Memory efficiency type, color, and texture are stored once per tree type, not once per tree. Three Oak trees at different positions use the exact same object.
Better performance fewer objects means less pressure on the garbage collector and better CPU cache usage. No lag when loading large maps.
Clean separation rendering data (intrinsic) and position (extrinsic) are completely separated. Changing how positions work never touches the flyweight objects.
Scalability a map with 50,000 trees might only need 5 flyweight objects, one per unique tree type. Memory stays flat no matter how many trees you add.
4. Practical Example: City Street Light Rendering
blocks.text: 4. Practical Example: City Street Light Rendering

blocks.content: Let's apply the Flyweight Pattern to a city simulation game. Imagine you are building a 2D city map that renders thousands of street lights across different districts. There are only a handful of distinct light types. Each type has its own name, color, and model, but every light also has a unique position on the map.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245782874-e83d67bf.png
Intrinsic state (shared) light name, color, and model. Identical for every light of the same type, so we share them across all instances.
Extrinsic state (unique) the x and y coordinates on the map. Every light placement has its own position, so this stays outside the flyweight.
Output:
Five lights installed, but only 3 flyweight objects in memory. The two Sodium lights share one object. The two LED lights share another. Halogen gets its own.

In a real city simulation with 100,000 street lights and 10 light types, you would have 100,000 StreetLight objects each holding just a reference and two coordinates but only 10 ConcreteLight objects storing the heavy color and model data.
That is the power of Flyweight in a domain where memory directly impacts how smoothly your city simulation runs.
